Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a post about starting a mentorship program on an engineering team. Around 250 words.

We started a mentorship program on our team last quarter. Here's what it actually looks like.

Six pairs, matched by what the junior engineer wanted to get better at rather than by who sat near whom. One person wanted to stop being scared of the deploy pipeline. Another wanted to write design docs that got approved without three rounds of comments. We asked for the goal in one sentence, and if someone couldn't write that sentence, we sat with them until they could. That conversation turned out to be half the value.

Thirty minutes a week, on the mentee's calendar, mentee-driven agenda. The mentor doesn't prepare. That was deliberate: the moment a mentor has homework, the program dies within two months. We've watched it happen twice at other companies.

The part I got wrong at first was thinking senior engineers would resist. They didn't. What they resisted was ambiguity about whether it counted as work. So we put it in the promotion rubric under technical leadership, named it in performance reviews, and the pushback stopped.

Three months in: four of the six pairs are still meeting. One pair fizzled because the mentor changed teams. One pair ended because the mentee got what she came for and said so, which I count as a success rather than attrition.

If you're starting one, my advice is to keep it small enough that you personally know how every pair is doing. Six pairs is about the limit for one organizer. Past that you need structure, and structure is where these programs go to become a quarterly survey nobody fills out.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- colon_reveal (That was deliberate:):
- colon_reveal (Three months in:):
- paragraph_uniformity (5 paragraphs, spread 0.30):

Return only the rewritten text.
